bu-he-biao-ge-bi-kuai: Her cousin came to visit with a model he had built. Hehe brought out her wooden tracks. She wanted their two vehicles to set off together.
She joined two straight pieces, then added a curve. Click—no, it would not fit. One corner of the curve stuck up.
Dad came over. “Look at your cousin! He can build something that complicated. Try to go a little faster.”
Hehe turned the curved track over, then back again. She did not want to try anymore. She pushed it to the bottom of the box.
“Mine is too simple,” she said. Her cousin was about to speak when Dad sat down beside her.
Dad thought for a moment. “I compared you with your cousin. You wanted us to play together, and I hurried you.”
“He knows how straight away,” Hehe whispered. “You have practised different things,” Dad said. “I'd like to see where you're getting stuck.”
Hehe brought back the curve. “This bit keeps sticking up.” Dad did not take it from her. He asked her to bring the two ends close together.
“This little bump goes into that little hole.” Hehe could see it now. She turned the piece halfway around, until the ends faced each other.
She held the straight track down with one hand and gently pushed with the other. Click! This time both pieces lay flat.
The blue train came along and stopped at the end. “We need one more piece.” Hehe looked into the box.
Her cousin offered a short track. “Will this one work?” Hehe checked. “Yes. The station can go here.”
They added a station together. Her cousin wanted a much longer track. “Let's keep it this long first,” Hehe said. “I want to try one trip.”
The train went around the curve without falling off. Hehe traced the new connection with her finger.
Dad asked, “What did you do differently this time?” Hehe held up both hands. “I know one hand needs to hold it still first.”
At snack time, Dad did not say who was better. He asked whether each child would like to show what they had made.
Her cousin talked about the model's wheels. Hehe talked about the little hole in the track. When she reached her station, her voice grew a little louder.
Before her cousin left, Hehe saved one loose piece. “Next time, I want to add a bridge right here.”
zhe-zhang-zhao-pian-xian-wen-wen-wo: Ningning made a hat from a big sheet of green paper. Its tip leaned to one side, like a leaf bending in the wind.
She put it on and walked to the mirror, wobbling with each step. Mum smiled. “I'd like to take a picture to show Grandma.”
As soon as the phone went up, Ningning pulled the hat lower. “I don't want my face in it.” Mum lowered the phone.
“Don't you want a photo today, or don't you want one of this hat?” Mum asked. Ningning took it off. “The hat is okay. Not my face.”
Mum nodded. “Then I'll photograph just the hat. You can look at the picture first and decide whether Grandma can see it.”
Ningning put the hat on a chair. The back of the chair was so tall that it hid half the tip.
She moved it to the low table. Mum crouched down. On the screen, a pair of little feet appeared beside the hat.
“Not my feet either.” Ningning stepped aside, and Mum moved the camera up a little.
Click. Mum showed her the picture. Ningning zoomed in on the tip. “You got the curly bit!”
She thought for a moment. “I'd also like a photo of my hands holding the hat.” Mum asked, “Would you like Grandma to see that one?”
“Yes. I'll put my hands like this.” Ningning spread her fingers along the sides of the hat, keeping her face outside the picture.
When it was done, the two pictures sat side by side on the screen. Ningning chose the one with her hands. “It looks as if I'm showing it to her.”
Mum checked again. “I'll send this one to Grandma. Shall I put it in our family group too?” Ningning shook her head. “Just Grandma for now.”
“Okay. Just Grandma.” Mum sent it and put the phone down. The hat went back onto Ningning's head.
That evening, Grandma called. “The tip really looks like a leaf! How did you make it bend?”
Ningning picked up the leftover paper and talked for quite a while. Grandma heard her voice and saw the picture she had chosen.
The next day, Mum wanted a photo of her reading in the hat. She asked first. “I want to read now,” Ningning said. “Let's talk about it later.”
Mum sat beside her and opened her own book. Sunlight fell on the green hat. Neither of them hurried to press the little round button.
wo-de-zhi-xiang-ming-tian-zai-chai: Xiaoman put a big cardboard box in the living room, with two smaller boxes in front. “My post office is open today.”
He put an envelope into a small box and took it out again. The big box still needed a letter slot. He wanted to make that tomorrow.
Dinner was ready. Mum tried to carry the bowls around the boxes twice, but could not get through. “This is blocking the way. We need to clear some space.”
Xiaoman spread his arms in front of the box. “Don't take it apart! I haven't finished.”
Mum crouched down. “You want to carry on tomorrow. I also need a path where nobody will trip.”
Xiaoman looked behind the boxes. “Can it go on the sofa?” Mum shook her head. “We need to sit there this evening.”
They walked around the room together. There was a little empty space by the wall, away from the door and the cupboard.
“Will the post office fit?” Xiaoman brought a small box to check. The big one still stuck out a little.
Mum asked, “Which part do you most want to keep?” Xiaoman patted the big box. “The letter slot is going here.”
The two small boxes could go inside the big one. Xiaoman took out the envelopes first. Mum helped him turn the empty box around.
Now it fitted. The big box stood against the wall, with a wide path in front. Xiaoman walked along the path to try it.
“How long shall we keep it here?” Mum asked. “Tomorrow after our snack, I'll finish the slot and tidy the leftover paper.”
They put the tape and paper into a basket. Xiaoman left one letter at the post office, then went to the dining table.
The next afternoon, Mum cut a slot where Xiaoman had marked it. He held the other side of the box, well away from the tool.
Xiaoman put a letter through the slot and took it out of the opening in the side. “Now both sides work.”
Mum posted a letter too. Xiaoman handed it back. For a little while, letters kept coming and going.
After their snack, Xiaoman gathered the scraps. “I'd like to keep it one more day.” Mum looked at the space with him, and they agreed to check it again tomorrow evening.
On his way to bed, Xiaoman did not guard the whole room. He touched the post office by the wall. There was still a little path for everyone to walk through.
ba-ba-ye-you-bu-hui-de-shi-hou: Guoguo opened his present. Inside was a shiny little harmonica. He brought the box to Dad. “Teach me to play that song!”
Dad picked up the booklet that came with it. “I've never learned either. Let's first see how to hold it comfortably.”
Guoguo paused. “You don't know either?” Dad nodded. “No. But I'd like to learn slowly with you.”
Guoguo held the harmonica upside down. Dad was not sure yet either. He pointed at the picture. “It looks as if this side goes on top.”
They turned it to match the picture. Guoguo held each end and gently brought his mouth to the holes.
He blew hard. The sound was loud and jumbled, and startled him too. Dad did not tell him to try again straight away.
Guoguo put it down and had some water. “Why did so many sounds come out at once?”
Dad checked the booklet. “If your mouth covers several holes, they may sound together. We don't have to play a song yet.”
Guoguo made his mouth smaller and gently blew a little air. There were still two sounds, but they were softer than before.
He tried once more. “The first one was louder, and this one was softer,” Dad said. “Could you hear it too?”
Guoguo nodded, with a little smile. Following the picture, Dad showed a slow outward breath with his hands. He did not use Guoguo's harmonica.
The next picture showed a gentle inward breath. Guoguo put the harmonica down first and tried breathing in as if smelling a flower.
He picked it up again and gently breathed out, then in. Oh! In the same place, the sound changed.
“One goes out, and one goes in!” Guoguo said. Dad heard it too. “We can both tell those two apart now.”
Guoguo tried joining the two sounds, but they became jumbled again. He looked at Dad. “I still can't play the song.”
Dad said, “Today, let's just listen to those two clearly. There's more to learn for a whole song. We can look for the next step another day.”
They cleaned the outside as the instructions said and put the harmonica away. Guoguo tucked a blue slip into the booklet to mark the page they had learned from.
That evening, Dad asked what he most wanted to remember. Guoguo thought for a moment. “When you don't know, you can still listen with me.”
wai-gong-zou-de-man-yi-dian: On Saturday, Xiaoyu put on her trainers. “Let's see the bridge in the park!” Grandpa picked up his walking stick, and Mum packed the water bottle.
At the park entrance, Xiaoyu had already run a few steps ahead. Mum called her back, and they walked together on the path where there were no cars.
Grandpa took small steps. Xiaoyu walked a little, then stopped a little. “Is the bridge very far?”
“My legs feel tired today. I need to walk slowly,” Grandpa said. Mum pointed to a bench ahead. “We can sit whenever we need to.”
Xiaoyu nudged a fallen leaf with her shoe. “I want to get there quickly.” Mum did not call her unkind. She took her little hand first.
“You really want to see the bridge,” Mum said. “Grandpa wants to sit outside too. Let's see how we can arrange both wishes.”
They sat on the bench first. Grandpa set his stick safely beside him and took his water bottle. Xiaoyu sat on Mum's other side.
Two chirps came from the tree. Grandpa looked up. “Listen. There it is again.” Xiaoyu stopped swinging her feet.
“Can you see it?” Xiaoyu asked. Grandpa pointed to a little grey shape among the leaves. He did not get up to chase it.
Xiaoyu could see its tail, but not its head. She sat and waited. The bird hopped down onto a lower branch all by itself.
Grandpa smiled. “Sometimes going slowly lets us see a little more.” Xiaoyu smiled too, though she was still thinking about the bridge.
Mum took out the park map. The bridge was far away. A big tree was nearby, with another bench underneath.
“Today I'd like to walk to the big tree and then go home,” Grandpa said. “You and Mum could see the bridge another day.”
Xiaoyu thought for a moment. “Let's go to the tree today. I want to see how big its shadow is.” Mum put the map away.
Mum helped Grandpa stand steadily. Xiaoyu waited until they were both ready, then walked along the shady path.
The tree's shadow covered the whole bench. Xiaoyu sat in it and held up her hand. “My hand feels cooler too.”
On the way home, Grandpa asked which day they would save the bridge for. “I'll plan it with Mum,” Xiaoyu said. “Today we saw that bird.”
That evening, Xiaoyu drew a tree with three people sitting underneath. She had not drawn the bridge yet. First, she gave Grandpa a place in the shade.
xie-dai-rao-guo-xiao-shan-qiu: An'an's new shoes had long laces. She liked the blue uppers and wanted to try the knot that looked like a butterfly.
Mum put one shoe on the table, pointing away. “Let's practise sitting down. We'll put them on after the knots have been checked.”
An'an straightened the laces and crossed them. She pulled them apart at once, and the crossing came undone.
Mum used the other shoe to show her slowly. “This end goes underneath, then you pull the ends apart.” An'an watched the little gap.
She held the crossing with one hand and passed the end through with the other. At last, a little knot stayed on the shoe.
“That's the first step,” Mum said. An'an untied it and tried again. This time Mum did not need to point out the gap.
Next, she bent one lace into a little ear. It was so big that it almost reached the toe of the shoe.
Mum asked, “Can you make it smaller and still hold it?” An'an slid the lace back and pinched the bottom of the ear.
The other lace needed to go around that ear. When An'an let go, the ear fell over and the other lace dropped too.
“I haven't got enough hands,” she sighed. Mum smiled. “We can just practise holding this bit today. Or take a little break.”
The next day, Mum showed her on the other shoe. One ear stayed up. The other lace went around it, leaving a little gap.
An'an asked Mum to hold the bottom of the ear. She bent a small section of the other lace and pushed that folded bit through the gap.
A second little ear appeared on the other side. An'an took hold of both ears and pulled. The knot tightened.
One side was long and the other short. She looked at it on the table. “There are two sides now. I'll try making them smaller tomorrow.”
A few days later, An'an started with the crossing again. An ear, a wrap, a gap—she paused to look at each step.
With the final pull, both ears stood up. They were still different sizes, but a little touch did not undo them.
After she put the shoes on, Mum checked the fit and the length of the ends. One end was too long. They adjusted it together before standing up.
By the door, An'an walked a few steps and stopped to look down. “It's still there.” She lifted her foot to show Mum the little butterfly.
kuai-zi-jia-zhu-xiao-tuan-zi: Lunch included Mingming's favourite stewed potatoes. The round pieces sat in his bowl. He put his spoon beside it and picked up a pair of short chopsticks.
One chopstick stuck out farther than the other. The tips would not meet. Mingming pushed a potato to the other side of the bowl.
“Why does it keep getting away?” Grandma sat beside him and set out her own bowl and chopsticks.
Grandma slowly lined up the tips. “First, make them about the same length. Hold them comfortably. You don't need to squeeze so hard.”
Mingming copied her, but the top chopstick slipped down again. He put it back, squeezing his fingers tighter and tighter.
“If your hand feels tired, relax it first,” Grandma said. “You can use your spoon when you want to eat.” Mingming took a spoonful.
After a few mouthfuls, his tummy did not feel so empty. He picked up the chopsticks again. “This time, I'll practise moving just one.”
Grandma showed him with her own chopsticks. The lower one stayed steady while the upper one moved gently. The tips opened and closed.
Mingming tried opening the tips without touching a potato. Both sticks moved. He stopped and settled the lower one again.
He tried once more. The lower chopstick moved less. The upper one opened like a little door.
Grandma asked which piece he wanted to pick up. Mingming chose a bigger one. He touched both sides gently, without lifting yet.
When he lifted, the potato rolled back into the bowl. “I hadn't caught it yet.” Mingming looked at the tips and shifted them a little.
This time, he gently closed the tips first, then lifted a little. The potato rose from the bowl, as if resting on a tiny bridge.
Mingming brought it to his mouth and ate slowly, sitting down. Grandma did not count his successful bites. She waited for him to finish this one.
The next piece fell again. Mingming smiled a little. “This one's too slippery.” He scooped it up with his spoon.
Over the next few days, sometimes he picked up two mouthfuls, and sometimes he only practised opening and closing. When hungry, he ate first. When tired, he used his spoon.
One day, a big potato piece reached his mouth steadily. Mingming said, “I made the lower chopstick stay still first.”
After lunch, he put his bowl and utensils on a tray. The spoon and chopsticks lay side by side. Tomorrow, he could use either one again.
jian-dao-yan-zhe-xiao-lu-zou: Duoduo drew a wide, winding road. A blue paper car waited beside it. She wanted to cut out the road and lay it on the table.
Mum brought her round-tipped children's scissors and sat down with her. “Watch where you're cutting. Keep the hand holding the paper away from the blades.”
Duoduo placed her fingers in the handles and opened and closed the scissors. Snip! A little cut appeared at the edge of the paper.
She hurried to push forward. The paper crumpled and the scissors stopped. “I want to get all the way there.” She pointed at the bend.
Mum brought a small strip closer. “Try this short, straight road first. Open a little, then cut a little.”
Snip, snip. Duoduo cut a little at a time. Slowly, the straight strip separated into two pieces.
At the end, the strip dropped softly. She looked at the edges. “There are little teeth here.”
“It's separated now,” Mum said. Duoduo saved the little road and picked up the paper with the curved line again.
At the bend, the scissors still wanted to go straight ahead. Duoduo stopped. “They don't turn by themselves.”
Mum showed her on her own paper. Cut a little, pause, then slowly turn the paper with the hand holding it.
Duoduo stopped the scissors and turned the paper a little first. The curved line came back in front of the blades.
She cut a little and turned a little. The edge was not perfectly smooth, but it began following the curve to the side.
She turned too far and cut a little notch in the road's edge. Duoduo looked at the notch and put the scissors on the table.
“My road is torn,” she said. Mum asked, “Would you like to carry on from here, or leave it for today?”
Duoduo touched the edge. “I'll carry on. It's still wide here.” She slowly finished the road, then put the scissors away.
The blue paper car went from the straight part to the bend. At the notch, Duoduo gently moved it a little farther in.
She drew a tree on some leftover paper but did not cut it yet. “Tomorrow, I'd like to try a gentler curve.”
After tidying the scraps, Duoduo laid out the road again. The car made a trip around it. She remembered too: her hand could slowly turn the paper.
hua-pen-li-de-yi-ke-dou: Mum brought home a little packet of bean seeds. Xiaochuan put it on the table. “What will they look like when they grow?”
Following the planting instructions, they filled two little pots with soil. Each pot had holes underneath and a tray below it.
Xiaochuan put one bean in the first pot and one in the second. Mum helped him cover them with the amount of soil the instructions showed.
A little water came from the jug, darkening the soil. Mum checked the trays. Together, they put the pots in a suitable place by the window.
They washed their hands. Xiaochuan drew two pots. “Today, there aren't any leaves yet.”
The next day, Xiaochuan ran to the window. The soil looked the same. His finger was about to dig inside.
Mum gently stopped him. “Digging it up would disturb it. We can look at the surface and check underneath for water.”
Xiaochuan crouched down. There was no standing water in the tray. He touched the surface, and a little cool soil stuck to his finger.
“It's still damp. We won't water it today,” Mum said. The jug stayed nearby. Xiaochuan drew a little water drop on his record card.
Another day passed. The window was still quiet. Xiaochuan asked, “Has it forgotten to grow?”
“Some beans take longer, and some may not sprout,” Mum said. “Let's follow the instructions for a few more days and see.”
Later, a little bump appeared in the first pot. Xiaochuan leaned closer. A tiny curved shoot was coming out.
“It's here!” Xiaochuan did not pull the shoot. He brought his record card to the window and drew a curved line.
The second pot was still quiet. He wanted to move it into more light. Mum checked the instructions with him before they chose a suitable position.
That day, the surface was dry. They slowly added a little water, paused to check, and emptied the extra water from the tray.
A few days later, the first pot had little leaves. The second still looked like soil. Xiaochuan drew their different shapes on two pictures.
Mum asked what else he wanted to watch. Xiaochuan pointed to a little leaf. “Will it grow another one?” They kept the second pot for now and carried on observing both.
Before bed, Xiaochuan looked at the window. No more water was needed today. He put the jug away and left the little leaf quietly until tomorrow.
feng-zheng-deng-yi-zhen-feng: Ningning brought a blue swallow-shaped kite to the open field. She spread both arms. “Today, it's going into the sky.”
Dad checked all around and chose a direction with nobody in the way. Ningning stood beside him until he said they could begin.
Dad held up the kite. Ningning took two little running steps. The swallow tipped up a little, then softly landed on the grass.
She wanted to keep running, but Dad asked her to stop steadily. “First, let's see if there's any wind.”
Dad took out a short strip of cloth. It hung softly down without blowing in any direction.
“The wind is very light now,” Dad said. Ningning looked at the swallow. “So it isn't that it doesn't want to fly?”
Dad smiled. “We need suitable wind. Let's have some water and wait a little.” They gathered the line and sat to one side.
After a while, the cloth gently blew in one direction. Dad checked the weather and their surroundings again, then stood up to feel the wind.
Dad chose their direction and held up the swallow. Ningning held the reel, standing steadily. The line was not wrapped around her fingers.
“Let out a little line first. When I let go, watch where it goes,” Dad said. Ningning watched the blue wings.
The swallow left Dad's hands and rose a little. Ningning was excited and let out too much line. It became slack again.
The kite wobbled and began to come down. Dad helped her reel in a little. “No hurry. Let's keep this bit steady first.”
Ningning turned the reel slowly, watching the swallow. Its wings swayed twice, then rose a little again.
“Now you can let out a little more,” Dad said. Ningning released a short length and paused, as if giving the swallow a path to travel slowly.
The wind grew weaker, and the swallow began to come down. This time Ningning did not chase it. “The cloth is hanging down too.”
Dad helped her reel in slowly and bring the swallow back to the field. They kept the line from trailing where someone might walk.
Ningning touched a wing. “It flew for a little while today.” Dad asked what she would check first next time. She held up the strip of cloth.
The swallow and the cloth were packed in the bag for home. Ningning knew her plan: next time, look at the wind first, then ask Dad if they could fly.
